item.title: China's APEC journey witnesses quarter-century pursuit of shared prosperity with wider world
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-18
This photo taken on Oct. 30, 2026 shows an APEC-themed digital poster at Shenzhen Bao'an International Airport in Shenzhen, south China's Guangdong Province. (Xinhua/Liang Xu)
SHENZHEN, Nov. 17 (Xinhua) -- Travelers arriving at Shenzhen's international airport this week are greeted by a message on screens: "Gather in Shenzhen. Witness the wonders."
Among the visitors are leaders and business executives attending Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) events. They are gathering in a metropolis that many longtime residents still remember as little more than a sleepy town amid rice paddies and oyster beds.
Nearly half a century after China launched reform and opening up, the changes set in motion have produced one of the world's most remarkable economic stories. Shenzhen is among its most striking chapters. And the miracle -- in the city and across China -- is still unfolding.
Shenzhen's rise began in 1980, when China made the small town next to Hong Kong a testing ground for economic reform. More flexible policies opened the door to investment from overseas. Local businesses began producing for international markets, while foreign goods, production techniques and management expertise flowed in.
The experiment proved successful. One indication came in 1991, when China joined APEC -- a milestone that highlighted how much the country and the wider world had to offer each other.
The Shenzhen meeting, scheduled for Wednesday and Thursday, will mark the third time China has hosted the APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting, following the one held in Shanghai in 2001 and the other in Beijing in 2014.
Over the past quarter-century, China has evolved from an emerging economy striving to integrate into the global system to an economic powerhouse and a major engine of growth. Its rise has helped create prosperity well beyond its borders.
An aerial drone photo taken on Oct. 20, 2026 shows a cargo ship sailing toward Yantian Port in Shenzhen, south China's Guangdong Province. (Xinhua)
OPENING UP
China's confidence in openness rests largely on its own experience. Shanghai, China's first APEC host city, offers two contrasting chapters in that history.
The Western-style banks and trading houses along the Bund testify to the city's early commercial prosperity. But they also recall a time when China found itself in an unequal position in the international order.
The city was forced open to foreign trade in the 1840s, after China's defeat in the Opium War. The conflict reflected how prolonged seclusion could leave a country vulnerable in a rapidly changing world.
After a series of military defeats and diplomatic setbacks, the Qing court was compelled in 1901 to sign a protocol with 11 imperialist powers. It imposed a heavy indemnity and granted foreign powers further privileges in China.
A full century later, China was engaging with the world on a very different footing. In 2001, Shanghai welcomed leaders of APEC economies to discuss trade, investment and economic cooperation.
By then, the People's Republic was more than half a century old, with a stronger economy and more developed institutions. There was plenty to fuel optimism that autumn.
China had just won the bid to host the 2008 Olympics, and talks on its accession to the World Trade Organization (WTO) had concluded. More than two decades of reform and opening up had reshaped the country and raised expectations for its future, both at home and abroad.
The photograph of Asia-Pacific leaders in traditional silk jackets became a defining image of the Shanghai gathering.
China joined the WTO that December. Liu Chenyang, director of the APEC Study Center of Nankai University in Tianjin, said China's APEC membership had helped pave the way for this step. APEC's flexible, gradual approach to cooperation and emphasis on voluntary action made it easier for the country to align its economic practices with international norms.
The country's accession to the WTO gave domestic companies broader and more predictable access to overseas markets. It also exposed China's own market to greater international competition.
In the years that followed, China became widely known as the "world's factory." From clothing and furniture to electronics, affordable goods made in the country found their way into homes around the world. Multinational companies reconfigured their production networks, more foreign investment poured in, and trade flourished.
For many Chinese families, these changes brought more job opportunities in cities, higher incomes, modern conveniences and better education for their children.
As economic globalization gathered pace, China benefited from overseas orders, investment and technological know-how. In turn, it offered the world a vast and highly capable manufacturing base and, increasingly, a fast-growing consumer market.
From 2001 to 2025, China's overall tariff level fell from 15.3 percent to 7.3 percent, a reduction that went well beyond its initial WTO accession commitments. By the end of the first quarter of this year, the cumulative stock of foreign direct investment in China exceeded 4 trillion U.S. dollars, roughly ten times the figure in 2001, data show.
Foreign investors have continued to benefit from their presence in China. Returns on direct investment have run at around 9 percent in recent years, among the highest in the world. In the first five months of 2026, foreign-invested companies reinvested 35 percent more of their earnings in China than in the same period a year earlier.
"China has been a great leader in the opening-up process," said Eduardo Pedrosa, executive director of the APEC Secretariat.
A NEW ERA
When APEC returned to China in 2014, the country's growing economic weight was already changing its relationship with the rest of the world.
The country welcoming leaders to the picturesque outskirts of Beijing was the world's second-largest economy and largest manufacturer. Yet the global recovery from the financial crisis remained uneven, regional conflicts had flared anew, and protectionism and unilateralism continued to cast a shadow over the international economic order.
China's development mattered far beyond its borders.
He Xilin, an assistant research fellow at the China Institute of International Studies, said the 2014 APEC meeting marked China's rise as an influential participant in regional cooperation, when the country began to play a more active role in shaping its agenda and advancing cooperation.
The Belt and Road Initiative, proposed in 2013, and the steps taken toward establishing the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank in 2014 reflected that shift. At the Beijing meeting, China pledged 40 billion dollars to help establish the Silk Road Fund, an initiative designed to improve connectivity.
The problems these initiatives sought to address were familiar to China. Better roads meant lower costs for farmers bringing their produce to market. Reliable electricity kept factories running. More efficient ports helped businesses reach overseas customers and compete for orders.
China had built such infrastructure on a vast scale. It was now seeking to share its experience with other countries.
The APEC meeting in Beijing was held under the theme "Shaping the Future through Asia-Pacific Partnership." It formulated a roadmap for a Free Trade Area of the Asia-Pacific, a vision first put forward in 2006, as well as the APEC connectivity blueprint for 2015-2025.
China's vision of building a community with a shared future for humanity gave the country's expanding international role a broader purpose, grounded in common interests and mutual support.
It envisages an open, inclusive, clean, and beautiful world of lasting peace, universal security, and common prosperity.
Workers use intelligent devices to customize production lines for clients at a workshop of Ningxia Juneng Robotics Co., Ltd. in Yinchuan, northwest China's Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region, Nov. 5, 2026. (Xinhua/Wang Peng)
Change was also underway at home. One year before the 2014 APEC meeting, China embarked on an unprecedented reform drive that reached deep into the economy and society, covering everything from industry and finance to public services, social welfare and environmental protection, in a bid to further unleash market potential.
Ahead of the meeting, authorities temporarily shut down heavily polluting businesses in and around Beijing to improve air quality. The unusually clear skies were dubbed "APEC blue." Chinese leaders pledged to make such blue skies a lasting feature.
More than a decade later, clear skies have become more commonplace, reflecting sustained efforts to curb pollution, upgrade the industrial structure and transform the energy mix.
China ratified the Paris Agreement on climate change in 2016. Today, the country supplies about 70 percent of the world's solar modules and 60 percent of its wind power equipment. It has also recorded the largest and fastest increase in forest area worldwide.
In September 2025, China announced its climate commitments for 2035, pledging to cut economy-wide net greenhouse gas emissions by 7 to 10 percent from peak levels, raise the share of non-fossil fuels in energy consumption to more than 30 percent, and bring total installed wind and solar capacity to 3,600 gigawatts.
The year 2014 was a pivotal year in China's poverty-alleviation campaign, following the introduction of a targeted strategy in November 2013.
The nationwide campaign lifted nearly 100 million rural residents out of poverty by 2021, eradicating absolute poverty in a country of 1.4 billion people. China thereby met the relevant target under the United Nations 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development a decade ahead of schedule.
The experience highlights several factors relevant to fellow developing countries: economic growth is essential for poverty reduction; investment in physical assets must go hand in hand with investment in people; and targeted policies can deliver better results than the even distribution of resources.
A container truck carrying the first batch of imports under China's expanded zero-tariff treatment to 53 African nations enters Shenzhenwan Port in Shenzhen, south China's Guangdong Province, May 1, 2026. (Xinhua/Mao Siqian)
SHAPING THE FUTURE
The choice of Shenzhen as the 2026 host offers a glimpse of how China is pursuing its next stage of development. Here, everyday life shows how innovation, openness and cooperation reshape the economy and create opportunities for others.
Over decades of manufacturing for markets at home and abroad, Shenzhen has built a tightly knit ecosystem that brings together component suppliers, engineers, mold makers and logistics firms.
Designs can be turned into prototypes in a matter of days, with materials and parts readily available nearby. The result is an unusually short path from concept to finished product.
Shenzhen-based Huawei, Tencent, DJI and BYD grew out of this environment, illustrating how such an ecosystem can nurture globally competitive companies. China now leads the world in producing more than 200 major industrial products and has built the largest and most comprehensive manufacturing system.
On factory floors, artificial intelligence is now changing manufacturing itself.
In a lithium battery workshop in Shenzhen's Bao'an District, an AI-powered system monitors production and automatically adjusts robotic arms to meet the industry's precision standards, eliminating the need to halt production for manual adjustments.
Such applications improve routine factory operations. But faster quotations, more precise production planning and fewer errors can also determine whether a company wins its next order.
Today, Chinese companies increasingly supply energy storage equipment, new energy vehicles, industrial automation systems and digital solutions overseas. Such exports often involve technical training and expertise in organizing production and building supply chains.
Beyond selling cars and building a factory in Cambodia, BYD provides training materials and instructors to help local educational institutions train more technicians.
China once benefited from the technology and expertise brought by foreign investment. Its companies now help other countries build their own production capabilities. Such ties extend beyond trade in goods, linking Chinese businesses' growth more closely with local development.
These developments are unfolding against a challenging global backdrop. Weak global growth has widened development gaps and heightened security risks. Rapid technological change is opening new opportunities while raising questions over ethics, security and the rules needed to govern its use.
China is seeking to do more to help address these challenges. In May, it implemented zero-tariff treatment for imports from 53 African countries, easing market access for their goods. In July, representatives of 29 countries signed an agreement in Shanghai to establish the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization.
From trade and technology to climate change and regional security, China's choices increasingly carry global implications.
The Shenzhen APEC meeting comes at a time when China's ties with the Asia-Pacific are closer than ever.
As the largest trading partner of 13 APEC economies, China counts eight APEC members among its top 10 trading partners. It also accounts for more than 60 percent of the region's economic growth, underscoring its growing importance to the Asia-Pacific's economic future.
From Shanghai to Beijing to Shenzhen, researchers have observed a pattern in China's hosting of APEC meetings: when consensus begins to fray, such meetings hosted by China often help bring economies back together.
As this year's host, China is looking to build on those ties and give regional cooperation fresh impetus. The Shenzhen meeting is expected to push forward the free trade agenda, draw on China's strengths in the digital economy and artificial intelligence, and help Asia-Pacific economies navigate technological transformation.
One key item on the agenda is closer coordination between the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership and the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership. Regional connectivity will also feature prominently, with leaders looking to build on work carried out under the APEC Connectivity Blueprint for 2015-2025.
In 2019, Shenzhen was designated by the central authorities as a "pilot demonstration area of socialism with Chinese characteristics" to develop replicable reforms for other regions in China.
China has set its own timetable: to basically achieve socialist modernization by 2035 and become a great modern socialist country in all respects by mid-century. Achieving these goals will further unlock China's economic potential and create more opportunities for countries around the world.
More than two decades after China first hosted APEC, the spotlight is returning to China. The world is looking for greater synergy to power the Asia-Pacific and beyond, translating the vision of shared prosperity into tangible progress.

item.title: Xi Focus: Xi calls for jointly building Asia-Pacific community to prosper together
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-18
Chinese President Xi Jinping delivers a keynote speech at the opening ceremony of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) CEO Summit 2026 at the Qianhai International Convention Center in Shenzhen, south China's Guangdong Province, Nov. 18, 2026. (Xinhua/Li Tao)
SHENZHEN, Nov. 18 (Xinhua) -- Chinese President Xi Jinping pledged on Wednesday that China is willing to work with all parties to forge ahead with resolve, jointly build an Asia-Pacific community and bring prosperity for all.
Addressing the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) CEO Summit 2026 in the southern metropolis of Shenzhen, Xi called on business communities in the region to uphold the entrepreneurial spirit and make greater contributions to economic integration in the Asia-Pacific.
Under the theme "To Prosper and Win the Future Together," the two-day summit has attracted more than 2,000 representatives from 21 APEC economies and 13 non-APEC economies, including Britain, France, Germany and Switzerland.
"The Asia-Pacific is our home; it is here we jointly pursue development and cooperation," Xi said.
Born amid the waves of economic globalization, APEC has been one of the world's most dynamic engines of growth. Today, the APEC economies are home to about 40 percent of the world's population, and account for more than 60 percent of global GDP and nearly half of global trade.
As the world becomes more turbulent and the global economy lacks growth momentum, the Chinese president said the region must answer the "hard questions of our times": to open doors or close doors, work together or against each other, adapt to change or stick to old ways?
In his response, Xi put forward proposals on how the region can prosper together, calling on APEC economies to uphold peace and stability, build bridges of opening up and cooperation, boost innovation to drive growth and expand ways for mutual benefits and win-win outcomes.
All parties in the region must "uphold the postwar international order," he said, calling on them to resolve differences through dialogue and consultation and address challenges through solidarity and coordination.
Xi said the Asia-Pacific should support free and open trade and investment while keeping the global industrial and supply chains stable and unimpeded.
"History tells us that opening doors brings progress while closing doors leaves one behind," he said, calling for efforts to steadily advance the process of the Free Trade Area of the Asia-Pacific.
He stressed the need to forge partnerships in science, technology and innovation, deepen cooperation in the digital economy and artificial intelligence, and promote green and low-carbon development.
"By doing so, we can turn strengths in innovation into drivers of growth, and provide strong impetus for economic growth in the Asia-Pacific," the president said.
The region should also remove trade and investment barriers to build an open Asia-Pacific economy, and promote development that is balanced and delivers benefits to all to ensure both efficiency and fairness, Xi said.
According to Xi, there is much to draw from the success of Shenzhen, host of this year's APEC CEO Summit and the 33rd APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting.
Over the past 40 years and more, Shenzhen has been a pioneer in China's pursuit of reform and opening up. It has achieved a historic transformation from a small border town into an international metropolis, creating a miracle in the history of global development, Xi said.
Noting that the Asia-Pacific region is home to the world's most important bay areas notable for their open and interconnected economies with positive spillover effects, Xi said China supports the establishment of a World Association for Bay Areas Economic Cooperation to deepen exchanges and interactions among bay areas from across the world.
"This will help us explore new ways for stronger economic cooperation in the Asia-Pacific," he said.
Looking ahead, as China's ties with the Asia-Pacific grow increasingly close, Xi said China's 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) provides a list of opportunities for promoting economic growth in the Asia-Pacific and the wider world.
The development blueprint is "an invitation for cooperation China has sent to business communities from around the world," he said.
Xi said China will provide the global business community with a super-sized open market, a promising land for development, as well as an environment that enables mutually reinforcing cooperation.
He highlighted China's accelerating efforts to develop a big, open market and build a modern industrial system, pledging a more stable and predictable first-class environment for companies from around the world to invest and do business in China.
Calling the Asia-Pacific business communities "pioneers of the global economy," he said they are "more than welcome to continue to get actively involved in China's reform and opening up and modernization drive, and share in the opportunities created by Chinese modernization."
Leaders of APEC economies, including Russian President Vladimir Putin, Chilean President Jose Antonio Kast and Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim, attended the summit.
Having previously hosted the APEC Economic Leaders' Meetings in 2001 and 2014, China is taking on the role of APEC host for the third time this year. It has hosted more than 300 APEC meetings and events this year and reached nearly 50 practical outcomes with other APEC economies in the economic and trade field.

item.title: Xi calls for advancing steady, sound development of China-ROK relations
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-18
Chinese President Xi Jinping meets with President of the Republic of Korea (ROK) Lee Jae Myung, who is in China to attend the 33rd Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders' Meeting, in Shenzhen, south China's Guangdong Province, Nov. 18, 2026. (Xinhua/Wang Ye)
SHENZHEN, Nov. 18 (Xinhua) -- Chinese President Xi Jinping on Wednesday called for advancing the steady and sound development of relations between China and the Republic of Korea (ROK) as next year marks the 35th anniversary of diplomatic ties between the two "friendly neighbors and strategic cooperative partners."
Xi made the remarks during his meeting with ROK President Lee Jae Myung, who is in Shenzhen to attend the 33rd Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders' Meeting on Nov. 18-19.
The two countries should uphold strategic independence, maintain the political foundation for bilateral relations, and further consolidate and develop the relationship, Xi stressed.
China and the ROK have substantially concluded the second phase of negotiations on the China-ROK Free Trade Agreement. The two countries should make full use of this institutional arrangement to strengthen macroeconomic policy coordination and foster a collaborative ecosystem for emerging technology industries such as artificial intelligence, Xi said.
China also stands ready to work with the ROK to facilitate people-to-people exchanges and carry out sound and beneficial cultural exchanges in a step-by-step manner, Xi said.

item.title: Xi welcomes Trump at Shenzhen airport
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-18
Chinese President Xi Jinping welcomes U.S. President Donald Trump at Shenzhen Bao'an International Airport in Shenzhen, south China's Guangdong Province, Nov. 18, 2026. Trump is in Shenzhen to attend the 33rd Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders' Meeting, scheduled for Nov. 18-19. (Xinhua/Yin Bogu
SHENZHEN, Nov. 18 (Xinhua) -- Chinese President Xi Jinping on Wednesday welcomed U.S. President Donald Trump at Shenzhen Bao'an International Airport in south China's Guangdong Province.
Amid welcome music, Xi and Trump shook hands warmly. Honor guards of the Chinese People's Liberation Army presented arms to salute, and a girl handed the U.S. leader a bouquet.
The national flags of China and the United States fluttered in the wind as a military band played the national anthems of the two countries, and fighter jets flew overhead in salute. The two heads of state waved to a welcoming young crowd.
Xi recalled his state visit to the United States in September this year, when the U.S. presidential couple came to the airport in person and hosted a grand welcome ceremony, noting that China is a nation with a tradition of courtesy that values reciprocating goodwill.
Extending his welcome to Trump for visiting China again, Xi said that he looks forward to conducting in-depth exchanges with the U.S. president on major issues concerning bilateral relations, Asia-Pacific cooperation and the global landscape to advance a constructive China-U.S. relationship of strategic stability based on respect, fairness and reciprocity.
Trump thanked Xi for greeting him in person at the airport and for the special arrangements by the Chinese side. He said it is a great pleasure to visit China again, calling China a great country and Xi a great leader.
Trump said that every meeting with Xi had been very pleasant, and he believes that the visit will further advance bilateral relations and achieve complete success.

item.title: Full text: Keynote speech by Chinese President Xi Jinping at the APEC CEO Summit 2026
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-18
SHENZHEN, Nov. 18 (Xinhua) -- Chinese President Xi Jinping on Wednesday delivered a keynote speech at the APEC CEO Summit 2026 in Shenzhen, south China's Guangdong Province.
The following is the full text of the speech:
Forging Ahead with Resolve
Toward a Bright Future for the Asia-Pacific
Keynote Speech by H.E. Xi Jinping
President of the People's Republic of China
At the APEC CEO Summit
Shenzhen, November 18, 2026
Distinguished Guests,
Ladies and Gentlemen,
Dear Friends,
Good morning! I wish to extend my welcome to you all, leaders of business communities of the Asia-Pacific. I am so delighted to meet you here in Shenzhen.
Shenzhen, on the shores of the South China Sea, embraces the surging winds and waves of the ocean. Over the past 40 years and more, Shenzhen has been a pioneer in China's pursuit of reform and opening up. It has achieved a historic transformation from a small border town into an international metropolis, creating a miracle in the history of global development. There is so much people can draw from Shenzhen's success.
Today, we find ourselves in a changing and turbulent world. Global growth lacks momentum, and unilateralism and protectionism are rampant. Still, global trade keeps growing against headwinds, and breakthroughs are being made in emerging technologies at a faster pace, exerting a profound impact on global development. What is going on with the world? What should we do in the Asia-Pacific? To open doors or close doors, work together or against each other, adapt to change or stick to old ways? These are hard questions of our times that we must answer.
As an ancient Chinese saying goes, all approaches should adapt to changing times to remain relevant. Born amid the waves of economic globalization, APEC has enabled the Asia-Pacific to steer the course of our times. This year, China is hosting APEC for the third time. We are ready to work with all other parties to forge ahead with resolve, jointly build an Asia-Pacific community, and bring prosperity for all in our region.
-- To bring prosperity for all in the Asia-Pacific, we should uphold peace and stability. There can be no prosperity without security, and no security without stability. Thanks to the stable environment in our region over the past decades, the Asia-Pacific has maintained steady economic progress and become an important engine driving global growth. The more complex the external conditions become, the more important it is for us to uphold the postwar international order, and promote an equality-based and orderly multipolar world and economic globalization that is inclusive and brings benefit to all. It is even more important for us to resolve differences through dialogue and consultation, and overcome challenges through solidarity and cooperation. This is the way to cement the foundation for sustaining peace and stability in the Asia-Pacific.
-- To bring prosperity for all in the Asia-Pacific, we should build bridges of opening up and cooperation. History tells us that opening doors brings progress while closing doors leaves one behind. We should firmly safeguard the WTO-centered, rules-based multilateral trading system, support free and open trade and investment, and keep global industrial and supply chains stable and unimpeded. We should work steadily toward a Free Trade Area of the Asia-Pacific, build a multidimensional connectivity network, enhance cooperation in areas such as digital transformation of trade, cross-border e-commerce, and smart customs, and deepen international cooperation on industrial and supply chains. All this will pave the way for greater economic integration in the Asia-Pacific.
-- To bring prosperity for all in the Asia-Pacific, we should boost innovation to drive growth. Innovation is crucial for progress. APEC members have driven global scientific and technological innovation: Unicorn companies and large AI models have emerged in large numbers, and many innovations have empowered hundreds of trades and industries and reached millions of households. We should forge science, technology and innovation partnerships, deepen cooperation in the digital economy and AI, and promote green and low-carbon transition. By doing so, we can turn strengths in innovation into drivers of growth, and provide strong impetus for economic growth in the Asia-Pacific.
-- To bring prosperity for all in the Asia-Pacific, we should expand our ways for mutual benefits and win-win outcomes. As the economies in our region differ in history, culture and stage of development, taking a uniform approach will not advance cooperation. We should remove trade and investment barriers to build an open Asia-Pacific economy. At the same time, we should promote development that is balanced and delivers benefits to all to ensure both efficiency and fairness. We should follow a people-centered development philosophy, strengthen economic and technical cooperation geared for developing economies, and deepen cooperation in transportation, public health, energy, food security, anti-corruption and other fields, so that development fruits are shared by all economies and all groups and communities.
The Asia-Pacific region is home to the world's most important bay areas notable for their open and interconnected economies with positive spillover effects. Shenzhen, where we are now meeting, is part of the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area. China supports the establishment of a World Association for Bay Areas Economic Cooperation to deepen exchanges and interactions among bay areas from across the world. This will help us explore new ways for stronger economic cooperation in the Asia-Pacific.
This year marks the start of China's 15th Five-Year Plan for economic and social development. China's economy maintains a strong momentum of high-quality, innovation-driven growth, demonstrating great resilience and vitality. In the first three quarters, the Chinese economy grew by 4.6 percent. New quality productive forces are developing more quickly, a new pattern of development is being fostered at a faster pace, and green and low-carbon transition is steadily picking up speed. The 15th Five-Year Plan has gotten off to a good start. A blueprint for China's development, the 15th Five-Year Plan also provides a list of opportunities for promoting economic growth in the Asia-Pacific and the wider world. Indeed, it is an invitation for cooperation China has sent to business communities from around the world.
-- China will provide global business communities with a super-sized open market. China is the world's second largest consumer market. It has the largest middle income group in the world and enormous potential for investment and consumption. From new energy vehicles to smart homes, from the silver economy to ice and snow tourism, every new growth area is creating new opportunities for businesses across the world. As China accelerates the development of a big, open market and increases import of quality products and services, more diverse demands will be unleashed. Recently, the ninth China International Import Expo was held in Shanghai. Many of you present today attended the Expo and found new cooperation opportunities. China will also continue to host "Export to China" series and other events to open efficient channels to help quality products from across the world enter the Chinese market.
-- China will provide global business communities with a promising land for development. Innovation-driven growth and green transition are the keywords in observing China's economy. From factory and farm robots, to autonomous driving and drone delivery, China is a super-sized innovation testing ground where frontier technologies are tested, improved and upgraded in real-world scenarios, and are then turned into high-quality growth drivers. China will step up efforts to build modernized industrial system, and deepen integration between technological and industrial innovation. It will support the transformation and upgrading of traditional industries, the expansion of emerging industries, and the forward-looking planning of industries of the future. This will generate strong impetus for technological innovation and growth of businesses around the world.
-- China will provide global business communities with an environment that enables mutually reinforcing cooperation. In 2001, China hosted the APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting for the first time and joined the World Trade Organization in the same year. Over the past 25 years, China has fully honored its WTO accession commitments. While pursuing its own development, China has shared opportunities with other countries and worked for common development. China has stood up to unilateralism and protectionism, and remained committed to true multilateralism, to upholding the multilateral trading system and WTO rules, and to advancing WTO reform; it has steadily brought stability and predictability to world economic growth and international trade and economic cooperation. No matter how the international landscape may evolve, China will not waver in its pursuit of win-win cooperation with all other countries. China stays firmly committed to high-quality Belt and Road cooperation, and welcomes the active participation of businesses from across the Asia-Pacific so that we can create growth opportunities and share the fruits of development together. China will not only cut tariffs and expand market access but also go a step further -- we will carry out reform in challenging areas, such as rules, regulation and standards, in order to fully ensure market access and an accommodating operating environment in the manufacturing sector, to steadily expand opening up in the service sector, and to foster a more stable and more predictable first-class environment for companies from around the world to invest and do business in China.
The Asia-Pacific is our home; it is here we jointly pursue development and cooperation. Asia-Pacific business communities are pioneers of the global economy. I hope you will carry forward the entrepreneurial spirit, boldly pursue innovation and excellence, explore and expand opportunities for business cooperation, and make greater contributions to economic integration in the Asia-Pacific. You are more than welcome to continue to get actively involved in China's reform and opening up and modernization drive, and share in the opportunities created by Chinese modernization.
Let us join hands to meet challenges facing development through opening up, generate momentum for growth through innovation, and pursue prosperity for all through cooperation. Let us work together to build an Asia-Pacific community and deliver a bright future for our region.
Thank you.
